chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-005.proposition: The tsunami raises a religious-pluralism problem because its victims held many faiths, while Christian exclusivism appears to deny salvation to many who suffered and died.

orphanFallback.rationale: Independently of any earlier opposing move, the victims' religious diversity and competing exclusivist claims challenge a common salvific explanation of their suffering.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-006.proposition: If an intelligent supernatural agent is interested in humanity, tsunamis and childhood cancers initially indicate that it is either malevolent or less than omnipotent.

orphanFallback.rationale: The observed examples of catastrophic suffering independently support an adverse inference about the goodness or power of any supernatural agent concerned with humanity.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-007.proposition: The proposed defenses create a dilemma: either God lacks the power to prevent suffering in a free world, or God can prevent it but permits it for a proposed greater good.

orphanFallback.rationale: As a standalone consistency test, inability to prevent suffering qualifies divine power, while deliberate permission requires an independently adequate account of divine goodness.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-009.proposition: An omnipotent God should be able to create free creatures in a world with far less suffering, so the claimed necessity of this world's natural evil requires unsupported modal assumptions.

orphanFallback.rationale: The conceivable combination of free agency and substantially less suffering independently places the burden on theism to establish why such a world could not be created.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-006.proposition: Appealing to unknown morally sufficient reasons for tsunamis and childhood cancer does not make belief in a caring and powerful deity reasonable.

orphanFallback.rationale: Without specifying how drowning or painful cancer serves a justifying good, bare trust in unknown reasons independently fails to reconcile severe suffering with divine care and power.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-008.proposition: Ordinary moral knowledge remains reliable enough to assess suffering despite uncertainty about remote consequences and chaotic causal effects.

orphanFallback.rationale: Everyday contrasts between helping and harming show independently that practical moral knowledge can remain dependable without exhaustive knowledge of all remote consequences.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-009.proposition: Future compensation for earthly suffering functions as a blank check, while the harsh facts of the world diminish the reasonableness of belief in an aware and influential supernatural being.

orphanFallback.rationale: The world's severe suffering independently counts against such a supernatural being when unspecified future compensation is offered without an account adequate to the harms observed.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-010.proposition: A world containing free individuals but no natural evil appears logically possible, so the theist must explain why it would be infeasible for God.

orphanFallback.rationale: The apparent logical compatibility of freedom with the absence of natural evil independently raises the unresolved question of why an omnipotent deity could not actualize that world.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-02.proposition: Objective facts about human needs, interests, sentience, and suffering can ground moral obligations without invoking God.

orphanFallback.rationale: Facts that humans need security, affection, and comfort and are capable of suffering independently generate moral demands responsive to objective features of human life.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-04.proposition: Natural facts about suffering constrain moral choice and provide a strong basis for mutual respect and kindness.

orphanFallback.rationale: A suffering person's condition independently makes helping preferable to further harm, illustrating how natural facts can constrain conduct and support respect and kindness.
